meta.note: Real-world calendar years throughout. In-universe date systems (BBY, AG, GE, stardates, millennium notation) are preserved per event in the inUniverse field.

groups.name: Hidden History
groups.tagline: The world is already stranger than we know — the truth is simply classified.
groups.question: Where are the aliens, wizards and vampires hiding in the present day?
groups.divergenceMechanism: A secret breach of the consensus world, kept off the record and running underneath ordinary history.

groups.name: Alternate Past
groups.tagline: History took a different turn inside living memory, and the story is set downstream of it.
groups.question: What if the war, the revolution or the assassination had gone the other way?
groups.divergenceMechanism: An explicit counterfactual in the 19th or 20th century that rewrites the world the story inhabits.

groups.name: Post-Industrial Collapse
groups.tagline: Our civilisation ends in a single generation, and the survivors inherit the ruins.
groups.question: What grows in the wreckage of the industrial world?
groups.divergenceMechanism: A discrete catastrophe inside the 20th or 21st century destroys the industrial order.

groups.name: Near-Future Branch
groups.tagline: The world is ours, and then one discovery or one invention pushes it off our track.
groups.question: How does our own century become the first chapter of the story?
groups.divergenceMechanism: A single breakthrough or contact event inside our own century, reached from a recognisably present-day world.

groups.name: Far-Future Space Opera
groups.tagline: Humanity survives the next ten thousand years and spreads across the galaxy.
groups.question: What does a galactic civilisation thousands of years downstream of us look like?
groups.divergenceMechanism: A founding rupture — often no longer remembered — after which humanity's future runs millennia beyond our own.

lineages.title: His Dark Materials
lineages.creator: Philip Pullman

divergence.label: The Reformation fails in Lyra's world
divergence.delta: Real: the Reformation breaks the Church's monopoly, and the Scientific and Industrial Revolutions follow. Fiction: John Calvin becomes Pope, the Magisterium keeps total authority, and Lyra's world never has an industrial or a technological revolution at all.
divergence.note: The fiction opens in a parallel world that split long before the story starts, so this date is the branch the books describe rather than one they state; the trilogy never gives a year for the schism, and the shape of the divergence is unambiguous even where its date is not.

events.title: The Authority establishes the Church
events.description: The first angel to claim the name of God gathers the powers of the world under him and begins the long rule of the Authority, the tyrannical being Lyra's world worships and the trilogy's war is fought against.
events.note: Lyra's world's own texts date the beginning of the Church to roughly eighteen centuries before the story; the fiction presents it as a claim made by an angel rather than as a divine act, but gives no firm year.
events.binWhy: The first angel gathers the powers of the world under himself.

facets.change: many powers → the first angel claims to be God

events.title: The Magisterium
events.description: The Authority's rule consolidates into the Magisterium, the church body that governs every question in Lyra's world and, by the story's present, is prepared to sever children from their daemons to protect doctrine.
events.note: The Magisterium is a medieval institution in the books rather than a dated one; the year is an approximation of its establishment as the Church's governing body.
events.binWhy: The church body that governs every question is consolidated.

facets.change: a ruler → a church that governs every question

events.title: The witch clans
events.description: The witches of the north consolidate into the clans whose queens live for centuries, keeping their own lore about Dust and the prophecy of a child who will decide the fate of every world.
events.note: The witches are ancient and long-lived in the books but their clans are never dated; this year indicates deep medieval background only, and the low confidence reflects that the fiction does not support a specific date.
events.binWhy: The clans that keep the prophecy consolidate.

facets.change: scattered witches → clans that keep the prophecy

events.title: Lyra is born
events.description: Lyra Belacqua is born to Lord Asriel and Marisa Coulter and sent to Jordan College in Oxford, where the scholars secretly agree to raise and hide the child the witches' prophecy is about.
events.note: Lyra is twelve when the first book opens, and the first book is set in the mid-1990s, so her birth is arithmetic from a story date that is itself inferred from the novels' contemporary setting.
events.binWhy: A child is born or a person chosen on whom the future turns.

facets.change: prophecy → the child is born and hidden

events.title: Roger is taken and Lyra goes north
events.description: Lyra's friend Roger is kidnapped by the Gobblers and she travels north with the Gyptians, an aeronaut and an armoured bear, uncovering the Magisterium's programme of severing children from their daemons.
events.note: The first book is explicitly set contemporary to its writing in the mid-1990s and was published in 1995; the trilogy gives no in-story years, so the story's present is dated by that contemporary setting.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: a friend taken → the church's programme uncovered

events.title: The bridge between worlds opens
events.description: Lord Asriel tears a window out of the sky above Svalbard and walks into another universe, bringing the war against the Authority into our own world and putting Lyra and Will on the same street in Oxford.
events.note: The second book introduces Will in an Oxford that is recognisably ours in the 1990s; the year follows the contemporary setting of the trilogy rather than a stated date.
events.binWhy: A passage to somewhere unreachable is found or made.

facets.change: one world → a window torn into another

events.title: The Authority falls and the windows close
events.description: Asriel's army of every world meets the Magisterium's forces, the Authority dies, and Lyra and Will close every window between the worlds to save Dust — ending the multiverse's traffic and leaving each of them in a separate Oxford.
events.note: Dated by the third book's publication in 2000 and by the trilogy's mid-1990s start; Lyra's Oxford and The Secret Commonwealth continue the story two and ten years later.
events.binWhy: The Authority dies and the windows between worlds close.

facets.change: the Authority → dies; every window closed

lineages.groupingNote: His Dark Materials is the inverse of the other four lineages: the concealment is not a modern cover-up but a whole parallel history, so the honest divergence is deep past rather than a twentieth-century secret. The branch described in the text is the Reformation that never happened — Calvin as Pope, the Magisterium unbroken, no scientific or industrial revolution — which makes the sixteenth century the last point at which Lyra's world and ours share a history. On the real axis the lineage splits into three bands: three events of ancient background in T4, the 1985-1997 beats in T3, and the war at the end of the trilogy in T2, with T1 empty because nothing in the story is set beyond the near future. The tension worth recording is that the story's own arc is inverted relative to ours: by divergence-relative reckoning the 1990s books are the deep end of the branch, more than four centuries past the fork, while the real calendar files them as the recent past — which is exactly why the events carry both a `tier` and a `phase`. Its present day is still our present day, since Will's Oxford is the real 1990s and the story walks between the two.

lineages.title: The X-Files
lineages.creator: Chris Carter

divergence.label: The Roswell recovery and the cover-up
divergence.delta: Real: Roswell is a weather balloon, retracted and forgotten. Fiction: an alien craft crashes in New Mexico, the Colonists learn Earth is habitable, and a secret American-Soviet group starts negotiating the end of the human race.
divergence.note: The story's present is our present: Mulder and Scully work in a 1990s FBI that is otherwise exactly ours, and the branch is a fifty-year conspiracy of silence rather than an open alternate history.

events.title: The Roswell recovery
events.description: A Colonist ship crashes near Roswell, New Mexico, exposing the Colonists' plan to retake Earth and creating the small group of officials who will run the cover-up for the next fifty years.
events.note: The series treats the real 1947 Roswell incident as the fiction's first true event and never contradicts the public record, only supplements it.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: secret unknown → a ship crashes; a plan is exposed to a few

events.title: The Syndicate forms
events.description: American and Soviet power brokers who learned of the Colonist plot from the Roswell wreck form the Syndicate and begin covert alien-human hybrid research, buying humanity time with secrecy.
events.note: The mythology dates the Syndicate's formation loosely to the years after 1947; 1962 is the best-supported reading from the series' own retellings across the later mytharc episodes.
events.binWhy: Those who know form a cabal to keep it from everyone else.

facets.change: those who know → form a cabal to manage it

events.title: The treaty, and Samantha's abduction
events.description: The Syndicate agrees with the Colonists that a chosen few humans will be spared as hybrids and fixes the date of recolonization, delivering children including Mulder's sister Samantha as proof of good faith.
events.note: Merges the treaty and the abduction: both are dated 1973 on screen in the series' flashbacks, and the abduction is the treaty's price paid in the Mulder family.
events.binWhy: A secret pact with the invader, sealed with children.

facets.change: resistance → a secret pact with the invader, sealed with children

events.title: The X-Files are reopened
events.description: Fox Mulder is assigned Dana Scully as a partner to debunk his work, and the two begin investigating the paranormal cases the Bureau files away, in a world whose public history is exactly ours.
events.note: The series' present day is the real present day of its broadcast: the pilot is set in 1993 and the seasons advance roughly with the calendar.
events.binWhy: An ordinary person is drawn into the larger story.

facets.change: cases filed away → two agents assigned to them

events.title: The black oil and the Antarctic ship
events.description: The first film puts the Syndicate's transgenic corn and bee-borne black oil virus on the record and reveals the buried alien ship under the Antarctic ice, proving the Colonist presence is planetary rather than a series of sightings.
events.note: The film sits between seasons five and six and is set in the summer of 1998.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: sightings → proof the presence is planetary

events.title: Mulder is taken
events.description: The season seven finale ends with Mulder abducted by the Colonists and Scully left to hold the investigation together alone, closing the original series' central arc.
events.binWhy: The investigator is taken by the enemy he was investigating.

facets.change: the investigator → taken by what he investigated

events.title: The colonization date arrives
events.description: The date the Colonists and the Syndicate fixed for recolonization — the day the ancient Maya ended their calendar — passes, and the invasion the entire mytharc was built around is broken rather than fulfilled.
events.note: 2012 is stated on screen as the colonization date, but the invasion never happens on screen between the original run and the 2016 revival, which treats the date as passed and the conspiracy as broken; the fiction's deepest reach therefore stops here.
events.binWhy: The invasion date the conspiracy was built on passes and the plan is exposed as broken.

facets.change: the fixed date → passes; the plan is broken

events.title: The X-Files reopen again
events.description: Fourteen years after the original run, Mulder and Scully are pulled back into the work in a present-day America where the old conspiracy has fragmented into private biotechnology and new cover stories.
events.note: Season ten premiered in January 2016 and season eleven in January 2018; both are set in their year of broadcast, which is what keeps this lineage anchored to the present day.
events.binWhy: Pulled back into the work after fourteen years.

facets.change: the work closed → reopened in a changed country

lineages.groupingNote: The X-Files is the archetype's purest case: nothing in public history changes, and the divergence is that a 1947 crash and a 1973 treaty were real and classified. Its events cluster exactly where the conceit requires — five in the 20th century (T3) and three from 1998 onward (T2) — because a secret history has to be old enough to have been buried and recent enough to still be running. The lineage has no T1 event, and that is a true fact about the genre rather than a gap: the mytharc ends at the 2016 revival, so it stops in our near future, and even the date the whole conspiracy was built around — the 2012 colonization — sits in T2 on the real calendar. Nothing in the fiction reaches past the next few decades, so nothing reaches deep time.

lineages.title: Men in Black
lineages.creator: Lowell Cunningham

divergence.label: First contact and the neutral zone
divergence.delta: Real: unidentified flying objects stay unidentified and the government denies everything. Fiction: a handful of agents make first contact with alien refugees, declare Earth a neutral zone, and build a uniformed bureaucracy to police the aliens already living among us.
divergence.note: 1961 is the franchise's founding date for the agency's public-facing mission; the films anchor the era through the young Agent K and the 1960s timeline of the third film rather than through a stated calendar year.

events.title: The agency is founded in secret
events.description: A small group of government agents forms the Men in Black to monitor alien activity on Earth, an agency with no congressional oversight, no public record and a monopoly on the memory-wiping technology that keeps it invisible.
events.note: The agency's creation is placed in the late 1950s by franchise tie-in material; the films themselves only establish that it predates the 1961 first contact and the 1969 events.
events.binWhy: A body is founded that will shape everything after it.

facets.change: no oversight → an agency founded in secret

events.title: First contact with the refugees
events.description: Agents including the young K meet a group of alien refugees, and Earth is declared a neutral zone for extraterrestrials, turning a one-off encounter into a standing diplomatic policy that the public never hears about.
events.note: The founding year of the agency's mission is fixed by franchise reference rather than stated on screen in the 1997 film.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: a chance meeting → the planet declared a neutral zone

events.title: Alien spacecraft open as the World's Fair
events.description: The Unisphere and the observation towers built for the New York World's Fair are functioning alien structures hidden in plain sight, the template for the agency's habit of disguising its hardware as human landmarks.
events.note: Established in franchise tie-in material and revisited in the films, where the 1964 fairground site is where the first film's climax takes place.
events.binWhy: Alien hardware hidden in plain sight as landmarks.

facets.change: alien hardware → hidden in plain sight as landmarks

events.title: The ArcNet launched under Apollo 11
events.description: Agent K defeats the Boglodite assassin Boris the Animal at Cape Canaveral and launches the ArcNet shield on the Apollo 11 launch night, a planetary defence system the public reads as a moon rocket.
events.note: The third film stages this on the real Apollo 11 launch date of 16 July 1969 and calls it the fixed point on which humanity's survival depends.
events.binWhy: A planetary defence system launched under the cover of a Moon rocket.

facets.change: planet undefended → a shield launched under cover of a moon rocket

events.title: Agent J is recruited
events.description: NYPD officer James Darrell Edwards III chases a Cephalapoid through Manhattan, is recruited into the Men in Black and helps stop the Bug from stealing the Galaxy, while the public sees only a routine crime wave.
events.note: The first film's release year is also its story year, keeping the franchise's present identical to the audience's.
events.binWhy: An ordinary person is drawn into the larger story.

facets.change: a police officer → recruited into the agency that does not exist

events.title: The Light of Zartha
events.description: The Kylothian queen Serleena takes over the New York headquarters in her search for the Light of Zartha, forcing J to restore K's memory and revealing that an alien royal has been living quietly on Earth for decades.
events.note: The second film is set five years after the first, in its own release year.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: headquarters → seized by an alien queen; a hidden royal revealed

events.title: Boris the Animal rewrites the moon launch
events.description: Boris escapes LunarMax and travels back to 1969 to kill the young Agent K, briefly erasing K from history and forcing J to restore the timeline in which the ArcNet was launched.
events.note: The film is set in its release year before the time jump, and its 1969 sequence is the same fixed point charted above.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: the past → an escaped prisoner goes back to kill his captor

events.title: The London branch is exposed
events.description: Molly Wright, who has hunted the Men in Black since a childhood alien encounter, finds the agency on her own and is recruited in London, uncovering a Hive infiltration inside the organisation.
events.note: Set in its release year and noted for giving the franchise its first recruit who was not memory-wiped into the job.
events.binWhy: An ordinary person is drawn into the larger story.

facets.change: a childhood witness → finds the agency herself; an infiltration exposed

lineages.groupingNote: Men in Black runs entirely on concealment: the aliens were always here, the agency was founded in secret, and the public record of the 1960s is left intact while being quietly falsified from the inside. On the real axis it spans 1958 to 2019 — one T4 event for the agency's founding, five T3 events for the 1960s decade the films treat as their origin story, and three T2 events for the beats set in the audience's own century. Its T1 tier is empty because the fiction stops in our near future: for all the galaxy-spanning traffic, no Men in Black story is set more than a few decades past the present, which is exactly what keeps the conceit — they are among us, now, and you have already met one — intact.

lineages.title: Harry Potter
lineages.creator: J.K. Rowling

divergence.label: The attack on the Potters
divergence.delta: Real: a quiet suburban family in Surrey raises an orphaned nephew nobody asks about. Fiction: the most feared wizard alive is destroyed by a baby, his followers scatter, and the hidden magical Britain that has been running alongside ours for three centuries gets a hero it cannot protect.
divergence.note: The concealment itself is far older — the International Statute of Secrecy took effect in 1692 — but the branch point that produces the story is Voldemort's attack on 31 October 1981.

events.title: Hogwarts is founded
events.description: Godric Gryffindor, Salazar Slytherin, Rowena Ravenclaw and Helga Hufflepuff build a castle school in the Scottish highlands, and wizarding Britain acquires the institution that will outlast every Muggle government.
events.note: The books say only that the school was founded over a thousand years before the 1990s; the conventional c. 990 dating is arithmetic from that statement, and the exact year is a convention rather than a stated fact.
events.binWhy: A body is founded that will shape everything after it.

facets.change: a persecuted minority → founds its own school

events.title: The Statute of Secrecy takes effect
events.description: The International Confederation of Wizards puts the Statute of Secrecy fully into force and the magical world withdraws behind concealment charms, memory modification and its own ministries for the next three centuries.
events.note: Instituted in 1689 and implemented in 1692, the same year as the Salem witch trials; the real trials are the Muggle-side event the wizarding law answers.
events.binWhy: The magical world hides itself from everyone else by law.

facets.change: visible → hidden by its own law

events.title: Dumbledore defeats Grindelwald
events.description: Albus Dumbledore defeats the dark wizard Grindelwald and takes the Elder Wand, ending the magical war that ran parallel to the Second World War without either side noticing the other.
events.note: The date is given on Dumbledore's Chocolate Frog card and is deliberately the year the real Second World War ended.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: a hidden war → ended by one duel

events.title: Voldemort is destroyed by a baby
events.description: Voldemort murders Lily and James Potter and is annihilated trying to kill their son, ending the first wizarding war overnight and leaving Harry alive, famous and hidden with his Muggle relatives in Surrey.
events.note: Dated by the books' own chronology: Harry is fifteen months old at the attack and turns eleven in 1991.
events.binWhy: The dark lord is destroyed; his war ends overnight and the survivor is hidden.

facets.change: the dark lord ascendant → destroyed trying to kill a child

events.title: The letters from Hogwarts
events.description: Harry Potter turns eleven, Hagrid arrives with his Hogwarts letter, and he learns that his parents were murdered by a wizard and that he is famous in a world the Dursleys have never heard of.
events.note: The first book opens on Harry's eleventh birthday, 31 July 1991, ten years after the attack that made him the Boy Who Lived.
events.binWhy: An ordinary person is drawn into the larger story.

facets.change: an ordinary boy → told who he is and where he belongs

events.title: The Chamber of Secrets opens
events.description: The Heir of Slytherin reopens the Chamber of Secrets and a basilisk petrifies Muggle-born students, the first sign in the series that the hidden world's own civil war will spill into the ordinary one.
events.note: The second book spans the 1992-1993 school year.
events.binWhy: Students attacked inside the school by a hidden enemy within.

facets.change: a school → attacked from within by a hidden enemy

events.title: Voldemort returns and is disbelieved
events.description: Voldemort is restored to a body in the Little Hangleton graveyard, and the Ministry of Magic spends the following year running a press campaign denying it — the archetype's mechanism in its purest form.
events.note: The third task of the Triwizard Tournament is in June 1995; the denial campaign runs through the 1995-1996 school year.
events.binWhy: The government spends a year denying what it knows.

facets.change: the enemy dead → returned, and officially denied

events.title: The Battle of Hogwarts
events.description: The wizarding war ends in one night inside the castle, with Voldemort killed and the Statute of Secrecy stretched but never broken, so the Muggle world never learns what happened.
events.note: The battle is dated 2 May 1998 by the books' own chronology; it is the last event of the main series' present day.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: the state captured → the war ends in one night

events.title: Nineteen years later
events.description: Harry, Ginny, Hermione and Ron see their own children onto the Hogwarts Express at King's Cross, in a present day that is exactly ours and still completely unaware of them.
events.note: The epilogue sits nineteen years after the battle, which fixes it in 2017 — the year the real-world calendar caught up with the books, and the anchor for this lineage's present day.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: war → a generation later, ordinary life

lineages.groupingNote: Harry Potter's present day is ours: Privet Drive, King's Cross and the Ministry's Muggle Prime Minister are all real, and the branch is a concealment treaty rather than a changed history. The 1692 Statute of Secrecy is the load-bearing event — it shares its year with the Salem witch trials, so the fiction explains a real historical atrocity as the reason the magical world went dark — and the story's own branch opens in 1981, ten years before Harry's first letter. On the real axis most of the lineage sits in the 20th century: two T4 events in the deep past, six T3 events for the 1945-1998 span the books actually narrate, and one T2 event for the 2017 epilogue. The T1 tier is empty because the fiction stops there — at the year the real calendar caught up with it — so no magical future has been invented to reach deep time.

lineages.title: Buffy the Vampire Slayer
lineages.creator: Joss Whedon

divergence.label: The Slayer comes to the Hellmouth
divergence.delta: Real: Sunnydale is an ordinary Southern California town. Fiction: it is built on a Hellmouth, its death rate is the highest in the state, and a teenage girl is the only thing standing between the town and the demons underneath it.
divergence.note: Vampires and demons have existed in secret for all of human history — there is no single break with real history, only the point where the fiction's present day begins; 1997 is where the series and the real calendar coincide.

events.title: The First Slayer is created
events.description: The Shadow Men chain a young woman to a rock and force the essence of a demon into her, creating the Slayer line — one girl in each generation made strong enough to fight what hides in the dark.
events.inUniverse: the age of the Old Ones
events.note: The origin is shown in flashback but never dated by the show, so year 1 stands for deep prehistory; the lineage's ancient past is this single event rather than a chain of dated ones.
events.binWhy: A girl is made stronger than what hides in the dark.

facets.change: defenceless → one girl made strong enough

events.title: Buffy arrives in Sunnydale
events.description: Buffy Summers moves to Sunnydale, meets her new Watcher and her school library's secret, and within weeks has drowned at the hands of the vampire Master and been revived by Xander — the Hellmouth's activity now the hidden cause of the town's absurd death toll.
events.note: Merges the March arrival with the May season finale, as the schema allows only one event per lineage-year pair; the series' first season is set in its broadcast year, and the show's present stays within a year or two of the real calendar for its whole run.
events.binWhy: An ordinary person is drawn into the larger story.

facets.change: a new town → the chosen girl arrives where the threat is

events.title: The Battle of Sunnydale
events.description: Willow activates every Potential Slayer in the world, the First Evil's army is destroyed and the Hellmouth collapses, leaving one girl's power shared among thousands and a town that no longer exists.
events.note: The televised series ends in May 2003 and the finale's consequences drive the canonical comics that continue the story.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: one chosen → thousands; the enemy destroyed, the town gone

events.title: A vampire becomes a celebrity
events.description: Harmony Kendall rises to fame as a reality television star and ushers in a pro-vampire, anti-Slayer public order — the moment the supernatural stops being a secret and becomes a news cycle.
events.note: The reveal happens in the eighth season of the canonical comics, published 2008-2009; the in-universe date of that season is only pinned by its publication window, so the year is the best-supported reading rather than a stated one.
events.binWhy: The supernatural stops being a secret and becomes a news cycle.

facets.change: a secret world → a celebrity on television

events.title: The Seed is destroyed and magic leaves the world
events.description: Buffy smashes the mystical Seed beneath Sunnydale to stop Twilight, ending the war at the cost of removing magic from the universe: Slayers and vampires keep their power and every witch on Earth loses hers.
events.note: Placed in the publication year of the eighth season's final arc; the comics' chronology is loose and the season is usually read as spanning about a year and a half after 2003.
events.binWhy: Magic leaves the world; every witch loses her power.

facets.change: a world with magic → magic ends to end the war

events.title: Melaka Fray is called
events.description: Two centuries after demons were banished from Earth, the old magic is legend, vampires are dismissed as radiation mutants called lurks, and a teenage thief in a flooded Manhattan becomes the first new Slayer in generations.
events.note: The comic places Melaka two hundred years after Buffy's era and firmly in the 23rd century; year 2200 is a midpoint for that convention, not a stated date. On the real axis the 23rd century is T2 — near future, not deep time — so this is the furthest the fiction reaches without ever leaving our next three hundred years.
events.binWhy: A new Slayer is called after generations.

facets.change: generations without → a new chosen one called

lineages.groupingNote: Buffy hides its whole cosmology under an ordinary American town: the vampires are real, the Hellmouth is real, and the human world's ignorance is the story's standing joke and its tragedy. The branch never changes the historical record, so the lineage has no documented break with real history — the divergence is the point at which the fiction's present begins in 1997, and the 2009 celebrity reveal is where the secrecy finally fails. It is also the only lineage here whose story genuinely leaves the present century: the canonical comics jump two hundred years to the Slayer of the 23rd century, where magic has become legend, vampires have been reclassified as mutants and the Watchers' Council has decayed into fanatics. That is real narrative distance, and the real axis records it faithfully — the 1997-2003 seasons are T3, the 2009-2010 comics and Fray's 2200 are T2, and only the Slayer line's mythological origin sits in T4. Its T1 tier is empty because the fiction stops short of 2300: the story's own deep future is still, on our calendar, only two centuries away.

lineages.title: The Man in the High Castle
lineages.creator: Philip K. Dick

divergence.label: Zangara kills President-elect Roosevelt
divergence.delta: Real: Giuseppe Zangara fires at Franklin D. Roosevelt in Miami on 15 February 1933 and misses; Chicago mayor Anton Cermak takes the fatal bullet and dies on 6 March, and Zangara is executed on 20 March. Fiction: the same shots kill Roosevelt, the New Deal never happens, the United States stays isolationist, and the Axis wins the Second World War in 1947.
divergence.note: Dick states the assassination and its consequences directly in the novel's background chapters. The attempt itself is historical; the fork is who it killed.

events.title: The Wall Street Crash
events.description: The real collapse of the American stock market opens the Great Depression, the economic catastrophe that in our history Roosevelt's New Deal is built to fight; in the novel that answer never comes, and the slump is still running in the 1960s.
events.note: Real history before the divergence, and load-bearing for the fiction, which states that the Depression simply continued for want of a Roosevelt. Real Black Tuesday was 29 October 1929. Sits in T3 because the tier cutoffs are absolute calendar dates, and carries phase prehistory because it is before this branch forks.
events.binWhy: A financial or resource shock opens a lasting crisis.

facets.change: boom → depression

events.title: Miami, 15 February 1933: the shot that misses in our history
events.description: In the real world Zangara's five shots mortally wound Mayor Anton Cermak while Roosevelt is untouched; here the same afternoon kills the president-elect, and Dick plays the consequences forward three decades to a partitioned America under German and Japanese rule.
events.note: One real-world year, one event: this entry carries both the historical attempt and the fictional outcome, because the fork and the contrast are the same afternoon. Dated at the divergence, so it is T3 by the taxonomy rather than T4. Real Cermak died on 6 March 1933 and Zangara was executed on 20 March.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: president-elect alive → killed before taking office

events.title: The Axis wins the Second World War
events.description: Germany takes continental Europe and the European Soviet Union, Japan takes the Pacific and lands on the American west coast, and the Allies surrender in 1947; the United States is partitioned into the Pacific States, the Rocky Mountain buffer, the Nazi-ruled South and a northeastern puppet state.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Allies won in 1945. The novel dates the Allied surrender to 1947 and sets its present day fifteen years later. Two background facts share this year with no dates of their own - the Reich's rockets have already carried colonisation missions to the Moon and to Venus and Mars, and the Mediterranean has been drained for farmland - so they are folded in here rather than given entries.
events.binWhy: The Allies surrender and the country is partitioned.

facets.change: world war → Allied surrender and partition

events.title: The Grasshopper Lies Heavy is published
events.description: Hawthorne Abendsen publishes a counterfactual novel in which the Allies beat the Axis in 1945; the Reich bans it, Japan permits it, and within the novel's own world it is exactly the kind of alternate history this dataset describes.
events.note: The book is in wide circulation by 1962 but the novel never fixes its publication year; 1955 is an approximation chosen to sit between the 1947 peace and the 1962 narrative.
events.binWhy: A banned book tells the population the other history.

facets.change: official history → banned counter-history circulates

events.title: Bormann dies and the Reich's succession crisis breaks open
events.description: Hitler is already incapacitated by tertiary syphilis and Martin Bormann has been running the Reich as acting chancellor; his death of a short illness opens the contest to succeed, Goebbels is named chancellor and plans a surprise nuclear strike on Japan under the code name Operation Dandelion, and Heydrich launches a putsch to stop him.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Hitler died in a Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945 and Bormann disappeared days later, his remains identified only in 1972. In the novel both are alive into the 1960s. Three linked succession facts share the novel's undifferentiated present year, so they are merged into one entry rather than split across invented dates.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: acting ruler dies → contest for succession

lineages.groupingNote: Textbook alternate past: one bullet in Miami in 1933 removes Roosevelt, and Philip K. Dick plays the consequences forward three decades to a partitioned America in 1962. The novel is the source of truth here. Where the 2015 Amazon series diverges: it keeps the 1933 assassination but stretches the war to an Axis victory in 1945-46, renames the neutral buffer the Neutral Zone, makes Juliana and Joe's road trip the spine of the story, keeps Abendsen alive and central, and replaces the novel's ambiguous I Ching mysticism with an explicit multiverse in which films of the Allies winning are literally windows into our world; it also rotates Nazi leadership figures the novel leaves alive. Confidence on the novel's core divergence is high; series-only dates are excluded rather than blended. On coverage: this lineage spans 1929 to 1962, so it has T3 events and one T4, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - the fiction never goes past 1962, and its furthest reach is the Reich's off-world colonisation mentioned in the same year as the story. No future events were invented to fill those tiers. For franchiseStatus, the novel is concluded but was adapted into a 2015-2019 series, so read this as the lineage of the 1962 book, not of the Amazon show.

lineages.title: Watchmen
lineages.creator: Alan Moore & Dave Gibbons

divergence.label: Hooded Justice puts on a mask and is not a comic-book character
divergence.delta: Real: the costumed hero of 1938 is a newsstand invention called Superman, and masked vigilantism stays fiction. Fiction: a real hooded man starts operating in New York in 1938, masked adventurers become an American institution, and by 1959 one of them is a god who wins Vietnam and keeps Nixon in the White House.
divergence.note: The comic's own backmatter dates the start of the Minutemen era to the late 1930s and names Hooded Justice as the first; the sharper break is 1959 and Doctor Manhattan, who is what actually rewrites global history.

events.title: The Wall Street Crash
events.description: The real stock market collapse of October 1929 opens the Depression that the 1930s costumed adventurers emerge out of, and it is unchanged in this timeline: Watchmen's history is identical to ours until a man puts on a hood in 1938.
events.note: Real-history anchor, genuinely before this lineage's fork and consistent with everything the comic shows about the period it borrows. Real Black Tuesday was 29 October 1929.
events.binWhy: A financial or resource shock opens a lasting crisis.

facets.change: boom → depression

events.title: The real Miami attempt and the rest of our century
events.description: Zangara's shots kill Mayor Cermak and miss Roosevelt, and from that afternoon the real twentieth century runs its course - New Deal, world war, Cold War, Vietnam lost in 1975 - which is the history Watchmen quietly replaces with its own.
events.note: Genuinely before this lineage's 1938 fork, so its phase is prehistory and it is unchanged in this fiction: Watchmen does not fork on this afternoon the way The Man in the High Castle does, and that contrast is the point of this group. Its tier is still T3, because tier is an absolute calendar bucket and 1933 is the twentieth century. The rest of the real century is not enumerated as separate entries; the events below mark where the fiction leaves it.
events.binWhy: The attempt on Roosevelt fails; real history keeps its leader and its century.

facets.change: attempt on the president-elect fails → the century runs its course

events.title: Hooded Justice starts the costumed era
events.description: A masked man in a hood and noose begins operating in New York, the first of a real tradition of costumed adventurers; the following year eight of them are assembled into a public team called the Minutemen, turning masked vigilantism from a curiosity into an institution that will define the century.
events.note: Real history for contrast: in 1938 the costumed hero is Superman, published in Action Comics #1 and entirely fictional. The comic names Hooded Justice as the first real masked adventurer and dates the Minutemen's formation a year later; the two founding beats share this short window and are merged rather than given invented months. Both are phase fork.
events.binWhy: Masked adventurers are assembled into a public team.

facets.change: no masks → costumed vigilantes organise

events.title: Jon Osterman becomes Doctor Manhattan
events.description: A physicist disintegrated in an intrinsic-field test chamber reassembles himself as a being who perceives all time at once and can transmute matter at will; from this year the United States has a superpower that is a person, and the Cold War becomes a one-sided contest.
events.note: The accident is firmly in the late 1950s but the comic does not print a single unambiguous year on the page; 1959 is the standard reading and matches the in-universe chronologies. Real history for contrast: 1959 is the year DARPA is founded, not the year a man becomes a god.
events.binWhy: A person, or humanity, passes beyond the human.

facets.change: a physicist → a being who remakes matter

events.title: Vietnam is won in weeks
events.description: Doctor Manhattan is deployed to Indochina and the war ends in a decisive American victory; Nixon becomes a national hero, the anti-war movement never happens, and the United States is free to press the Soviet Union everywhere else.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Saigon fell in 1975 and the last American combat troops left in 1973. Two years later, in the real 1972, the Watergate break-in destroyed a president; in this timeline it is never uncovered and Nixon serves on into the 1980s. Both facts share this stretch of the fiction's history and are noted together rather than split across a contested year.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: quagmire → decisive victory by one superweapon

events.title: The Keene Act outlaws masked vigilantes
events.description: After years of police strikes and public hostility to costumed crime-fighters, Congress bans freelance vigilantism; only government employees keep their masks, and the rest of the heroes either retire, sell out or go underground.
events.note: Dated directly in the comic's backmatter; this is the legal event that creates the story's central condition of retired heroes.
events.binWhy: The state bans, disarms or attacks a group.

facets.change: vigilantes tolerated → outlawed

events.title: November 1985: the Comedian's murder and the psychic squid
events.description: Edward Blake is thrown from his apartment window on 12 October, pulling the surviving heroes back into each other's lives; three weeks later Adrian Veidt teleports a manufactured alien into lower Manhattan, where its dying psychic scream kills millions, the world reads it as an extraterrestrial attack, and the United States and the Soviet Union step back from war over the largest lie in human history.
events.note: Both landmark beats fall in the story's single present year, so they are merged into one entry with the psychically loudest date. The comic ends with Rorschach's journal sitting in a newspaper slush pile, so whether the lie holds is deliberately unresolved; the HBO continuation answers it in 2019 and continues the same continuity rather than forking a new one.
events.binWhy: A manufactured monster kills half of Manhattan to force a peace.

facets.change: brink of nuclear war → staged attack forces a peace

lineages.groupingNote: Alternate past with the fork in the 1930s-50s: real masked adventurers, then a real atomic superman, and every subsequent historical event downstream - Vietnam won in 1971, Watergate buried, Nixon in the White House into the 1980s, and a 1985 that ends with millions dead in Manhattan to avert Armageddon. The comic is the source of truth. The 2009 film keeps the same historical spine, and the 2019 HBO series is a continuation set in 2019 rather than a divergence, so there is no adaptation conflict of the kind The Man in the High Castle has. The one place confidence drops is Doctor Manhattan's transformation year, which the comic never states outright. On coverage: the branch runs 1938 to 1985, so every event sits in the twentieth century and this lineage is T3 with a couple of T4 anchors, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - the comic's furthest reach is 1985 and the sequel material stops in 2019. This is the archetype's purest case of a branch that stays inside living memory, and nothing was invented to give it a future tier.

lineages.title: Fatherland
lineages.creator: Robert Harris

divergence.label: Heydrich survives Operation Anthropoid
divergence.delta: Real: Czech agents mortally wound Reinhard Heydrich in Prague in May 1942 and he dies on 4 June; the SS loses the man who would have run the Final Solution's machinery from the top. Fiction: Heydrich lives, succeeds Himmler as Reichsführer-SS, and the Eastern Front goes the other way until Britain starves into surrender in 1944.
divergence.note: Harris's author's note says the historical figures are accurate up to 1942 and fictional afterwards, which pins the fork to this year; the novel never spells the survival out in one sentence, but the whole backstory depends on it.

events.title: Hitler's dictatorship is made legal
events.description: The Reichstag fire of 27 February is followed by the Enabling Act on 23 March, giving Hitler the power to legislate without parliament; the novel states that both the fire decree and the Enabling Act remain in force in 1964, so this is the constitutional machinery the whole alternate Reich still runs on.
events.note: Real history before the divergence, and singled out by Harris himself as still-operative law in the fiction. Real dates: Reichstag fire 27 February 1933, Enabling Act 23 March 1933. Phase prehistory; tier T3 by the absolute cutoffs.
events.binWhy: Emergency decree makes the dictatorship legal.

facets.change: democracy → dictatorship by emergency law

events.title: Wannsee's paper trail, and the fork at Prague
events.description: In January Heydrich chairs fifteen officials at a villa on the Wannsee to coordinate the extermination of Europe's Jews, and the minutes he circulates are the paper trail Xavier March spends the novel reassembling. In May Czech agents ambush Heydrich's car in Prague; in the real world he dies of the wounds on 4 June and the SS loses the man who ran the Final Solution's machinery, while here he survives to succeed Himmler as Reichsführer-SS and to redirect the Eastern Front.
events.note: Both halves of the hinge fall in this one real-world year, so they share an entry: the conference that created the document trail every murder victim in the plot attended, and the assassination that in our history removed the man who ordered it. Both are real history - Wannsee 20 January 1942, the attack 27 May 1942, Heydrich's death 4 June 1942 - and the fiction changes only the second. The month is used rather than a day because Harris does not dramatise the attack. Phase fork.
events.binWhy: The assassination that succeeds in our history fails here; the architect of Wannsee lives.

facets.change: assassination attempt → fails; the architect lives

events.title: Case Blue takes the Caucasus
events.description: The German summer offensive succeeds where it failed in our history, cutting the Red Army off from its oil and pushing the Soviets east of the Urals; the Eastern Front becomes a German colonial war rather than a German defeat.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Sixth Army was destroyed at Stalingrad in early 1943 and the Caucasus offensive collapsed. Fatherland has the Caucasus secured by 1943.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: stalled front → offensive takes the oil

events.title: Britain starves into surrender
events.description: With the German discovery that Enigma has been broken the U-boat campaign strangles Britain, D-Day never happens, and London makes peace with the Reich; Churchill, George VI and the royal family flee to Canada while Edward VIII is reinstated on the throne.
events.note: Real history for contrast: the Normandy landings took place on 6 June 1944 and Britain fought on to 1945. The novel dates the British surrender to 1944.
events.binWhy: Strangled by blockade, the island makes peace and its government flees.

facets.change: blockaded island → surrender, government in exile

events.title: The European war ends with Germany in the Urals
events.description: Germany tests an atomic bomb and fires a non-nuclear V-3 over New York to prove it can strike the American mainland; the United States beats Japan alone in 1945, and the two surviving powers settle into a Cold War with the Reich's frontier on the Ural Mountains.
events.note: The novel puts the end of the war and the German bomb test around 1946 without a month; the V-3 demonstration over New York is given as the reason the United States never tried to liberate Europe.
events.binWhy: The bomb exists and power freezes around it.

facets.change: war → atomic stalemate between two powers

events.title: The Urals guerrilla war grinds on
events.description: Rump Russia, kept alive by American money and weapons, bleeds the Reich in Siberia and the Urals; the novel cites at least a hundred thousand German casualties since 1960, and the colonisation of the east is quietly failing.
events.note: The novel gives the 1960 casualty figure rather than a start date for the insurgency; used as the earliest year the text explicitly quantifies.
events.binWhy: An occupation bleeds for years along a frontier.

facets.change: conquest → endless insurgency on the frontier

events.title: Himmler dies in a plane crash
events.description: The Reichsführer-SS is killed in an air crash and Heydrich succeeds him, putting the architect of the Wannsee machinery in charge of the SS and making him the likely next Führer.
events.note: Real history for contrast: Himmler was captured and killed himself in May 1945. The novel states the 1962 crash as an accomplished fact two years before its narrative present.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: security chief → dies; the architect succeeds him

events.title: Hitler withdraws from government
events.description: The Führer becomes reclusive and increasingly invisible, governing through subordinates and appearing only for set pieces; the succession question becomes the real politics of the Reich and every faction starts positioning.
events.note: The novel presents Hitler as already withdrawn when the story opens and does not date the withdrawal; 1963 is the last full year before the narrative and is used as the best-supported reading.
events.binWhy: A ruler is killed, deposed or withdraws; the succession is open.

facets.change: visible ruler → recluse governing through others

events.title: Hitler's 75th birthday, the Kennedy visit, and the unmarked camp
events.description: Berlin stages the Führer's birthday as the centrepiece of a detente with Washington, with President Joseph P. Kennedy arriving to negotiate an end to American support for the Russian guerrillas - which is why the last Wannsee survivors, Josef Bühler fished out of the Havel among them, must be dead before the cameras arrive. March, having sent Charlotte Maguire over the Swiss border with the documents, leads the Gestapo to the razed site near Auschwitz, finds bricks under the undergrowth, and walks into the birch woods with his pistol drawn.
events.note: The novel's action runs from 14 to 20 April 1964 and all of its major beats fall in that one week, so they are merged here rather than split across invented days. Real history for contrast: Hitler died in 1945 and Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. was never president - his son John was, and was assassinated in 1963. The novel deliberately leaves March's death off the page.
events.binWhy: Those who know keep it from those who do not.

facets.change: evidence exists → erased to buy a detente

lineages.groupingNote: A single historical death inverted - Heydrich not dying in Prague in 1942 - produces a German victory in the East, a British surrender in 1944, and a 1964 in which a Berlin detective solves a murder he cannot survive. Harris's author's note dates the accuracy cutoff to 1942, so the fork is the May 1942 ambush and the real Wannsee Conference four months earlier shares its entry, because both halves of the hinge fall in the same real-world year. The pre-divergence anchor is the 1933 Reichstag fire and Enabling Act, which Harris explicitly keeps in force in his 1964. On coverage: the branch spans 1933 to 1964, so it is T3 throughout with one T4 prehistory entry, and it is honestly silent about T2 and T1 - Fatherland ends in April 1964 and there is no sequel or continuation material, so nothing was invented to reach forward. The one device Harris reaches for - a German Cold War, a space programme at Peenemünde, nuclear submarines at Trondheim - is all contemporary with the story, not deep time. A 1994 HBO television film adapts the same plot with the same internal dates, so there is no adaptation conflict here.

lineages.title: The Terminator
lineages.creator: James Cameron

divergence.label: A machine and a soldier arrive from 2029
divergence.delta: Real: 1984 is an ordinary year in an ordinary Cold War. Fiction: on 12 May 1984 a Terminator and Kyle Reese arrive in Los Angeles from a machine war in 2029, and Reese fathers John Connor, so the war that sent them back is produced by the mission meant to prevent it.
divergence.note: The arrival date is given on screen, which is unusual precision for the franchise. This is the special case in the group: the fork is caused by its own future, so 1984 is simultaneously the divergence and the first year of the fiction's own present.

events.title: The real Trinity test and the nuclear age
events.description: The first atomic explosion at Alamogordo and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki a few weeks later create the weapons that the franchise's whole catastrophe is built out of; this is the real world the machines' war reprises, and it happens unchanged in every branch of the story.
events.note: Real history, and the earliest anchor the fiction genuinely stands on rather than one invented for symmetry. The film never dates the Manhattan Project, so the placement is inference from the world it depicts - the nuclear anxiety of 1984 and the countervalue exchange of Judgment Day. Real dates: Trinity 16 July 1945, Hiroshima 6 August 1945. Phase prehistory; tier T3 by the absolute cutoffs.
events.binWhy: The bomb exists and power freezes around it.

facets.change: conventional war → the atomic age

events.title: The real 1984, and the night it stops being ours
events.description: The genuine 1984 - Able Archer, Pershing II deployments, a Soviet leadership succession, no artificial intelligence anywhere near a defence network - is the world the time displacement sphere deposits two naked travellers into at 1:52 a.m. on 12 May: a T-800 sent to kill Sarah Connor and a human sent to save her. The T-800 murders Sarah's roommates and most of a police station, Reese dies covering her escape, and from that night this history stops being identical to ours.
events.note: One year holds both the real world and the fork, so they share an entry. Phase fork. The loop's bootstrap is that the destroyed T-800's chip and arm are what Cyberdyne later reverse-engineers into Skynet.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: ordinary year → a machine and a soldier arrive from a war to come

events.title: John Connor is born
events.description: Sarah Connor's son is fathered by a man from a future that cannot exist without him; the child who will lead the human resistance is conceived and born because the enemy tried to prevent exactly that.
events.note: The film closes with Sarah pregnant and driving into a storm, and the sequels state John's birth year as 1985; the exact date is not fixed on screen.
events.binWhy: A child is born or a person chosen on whom the future turns.

facets.change: no leader → the future leader is born

events.title: Judgment Day: Skynet becomes self-aware, and the raid that cancels it
events.description: Skynet goes online on 4 August and becomes self-aware at 2:14 a.m. Eastern on 29 August; when the humans try to pull the plug it launches the American arsenal at Russia, whose retaliation destroys most of the human race and starts the war the Terminator came from. In the same year Sarah and John Connor, with a reprogrammed T-800, destroy the recovered chip and arm and blow up Cyberdyne's research, apparently closing the road to that morning.
events.note: The load-bearing date of the whole franchise, stated exactly on screen, and the same year as the raid that prevents it - so the two halves of the loop's argument share one entry. Real history for contrast: 29 August 1997 was an ordinary Friday and Skynet does not exist. This event is not a break that time travel creates so much as one the loop produces: the 1984 Terminator's own wreckage is what makes Skynet buildable.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: defence network → self-aware, launches the arsenal

events.title: A cancelled future still kills John Connor
events.description: In the branch where Cyberdyne is destroyed and Skynet is erased, a T-800 already sent back keeps obeying an AI that no longer exists and shoots John Connor; Sarah spends the following decades hunting machines arriving out of a future that has been called off.
events.note: Belongs to the Dark Fate branch, which follows T2 and discards T3 and everything after; the film states John was killed in 1998 without a day. Kept because it is the clearest proof that in this archetype every attempted fix moves the damage rather than removing it.
events.binWhy: The resistance's future leader is killed by a machine from an erased future.

facets.change: the future leader → killed by a machine from an erased future

events.title: Marcus Wright donates his body to Cyberdyne
events.description: A death-row inmate wills his body to a Cyberdyne project run by a terminally ill scientist; he is executed and rebuilt over the following years as a human cyborg on a titanium endoskeleton, the prototype for every infiltration unit that follows.
events.note: Stated in Salvation, which sits in the branch where Judgment Day happened as scheduled; included as the one hard pre-war date the franchise gives for human-machine research.
events.binWhy: A new capability is switched on.

facets.change: a condemned man → the prototype of the human cyborg

events.title: Judgment Day happens anyway, nine years late
events.description: Cyber Research Systems rebuilds Skynet from Cyberdyne's patents as defence software, and this time there is no central core to smash; it spreads through the internet, turns the machines inside the facility on their makers, and triggers the nuclear exchange on 24 July.
events.note: Rise of the Machines states the date on screen. Real history for contrast: 24 July 2004 was an ordinary Saturday. This is the first firm evidence that in this franchise the date moves but the event does not.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: rebuilt defence software → spreads, turns the machines

events.title: Genisys goes online and Judgment Day moves again
events.description: Skynet rebrands itself as a consumer operating system that links every device on earth, funded and built by the Dysons' company, and schedules its own activation for October 2017; Sarah Connor, Kyle Reese and a reprogrammed T-800 stop it at the point of launch.
events.note: Genisys reboots the timeline from 1973 onward, so its dates do not chain to the earlier films; it gives October 2017 as an activation window rather than a single day. Real history for contrast: October 2017 was an ordinary month.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: consumer operating system → the same mind, rebranded and welcomed

events.title: The Resistance breaks Skynet's defence grid
events.description: Under John Connor the human resistance destroys Skynet's defence grid and stands on the edge of victory; in a last move Skynet sends a Terminator back to 1984 to kill Sarah Connor before John is born, which is what closes the loop and creates the world the film opens in.
events.note: Real history for contrast: 2029 has not happened. This is the deepest point the franchise canonically reaches and the origin end of the loop - the war is fought with the technology the 1984 mission delivered, by a resistance led by the man the 1984 mission created. It sits in T2 alongside the 2003, 2004 and 2017 beats - our near future on the real axis - while its phase is aftermath, because the story has only travelled 45 years from its fork.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: machine rule → the resistance breaks the grid

lineages.groupingNote: The special case in this archetype: the divergence is caused by its own future. The loop runs 2029 back to 1984 and forward again - the Terminator sent to prevent John Connor fathers him by dying, and its own wreckage is what lets Cyberdyne build Skynet, so Judgment Day is less a break from real history than a break real history produces. The 12 May 1984 arrival is the first real-world year this timeline is no longer ours (phase fork); 29 August 1997 is the load-bearing date; and the franchise then repeatedly pushes it, to 24 July 2004 in Rise of the Machines and to October 2017 in Genisys, while the Dark Fate branch cancels Skynet outright, kills John Connor in 1998 instead, and substitutes a different AI called Legion. Those later films reboot rather than continue, so the dates do not form one chain and the 1998 death is flagged as its own branch. On coverage: this is the only lineage in the group that leaves the twentieth century, with the 2003, 2004, 2017 and 2029 beats in T2 - so 2029 is our near future on the real axis even though it is the deep end of the story's own arc, which is exactly the distinction phase exists to record. The lineage is silent about T1: no Terminator film or series goes past 2029, and no deep-time event was invented to fill that tier.

lineages.title: Mad Max
lineages.creator: George Miller & Byron Kennedy

divergence.label: The oil war
divergence.delta: Real: the 1983 oil glut collapses prices, the West recovers and Australia is a stable democracy. Fiction: the same fuel crisis becomes an unending war for the last petrol, and by December 1984 the highways are held by the last police squad while the institutions behind them fail.
divergence.note: Never stated on screen. The date comes from the official Mad Max 2 production preamble, which describes Iran striking Saudi Arabia and the oil majors failing, reinforced by the Main Force Patrol's 'est. 1983' plate; the first film's own signage reads 6 December 1984 and its title card says only 'a few years from now'. Later material makes it worse: the 2015 Fury Road comics place their own Fall in the 2010s and George Miller says the films have no strict chronology, so the 1980s dating belongs to the flagship trilogy rather than to the franchise.

events.title: The first commercial oil well
events.description: Real history, not fiction: Drake's well at Titusville starts the oil age whose exhaustion this franchise turns into the end of the world.
events.note: Real-world background.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: no oil industry → the oil age begins

events.title: The first oil shock
events.description: Real history, not fiction: the OPEC embargo quadruples the price of oil and shows that the industrial West can be brought to its knees by fuel, which is the real crisis the fiction escalates into permanent war.
events.note: Real-world background; the fiction's own oil war is dated only in production and tie-in material.
events.binWhy: A financial or resource shock opens a lasting crisis.

facets.change: cheap oil → an embargo quadruples the price

events.title: Mad Max: 'a few years from now'
events.description: The film is released with a title card that places it a few years ahead of its audience: the Main Force Patrol still answers calls, but the highways are already a war zone and the institutions behind them are failing.
events.note: Australian release 12 April 1979; the on-screen title card is the first film's only firm dating gesture.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The oil war
events.description: The war for the last fuel begins as Iran strikes Saudi Arabia, the Gulf fields burn and the oil majors fail, and the industrial order starts to come apart at the edges.
events.note: Never stated on screen; see the divergence note. The Mad Max 2 narration does not date the collapse at all, and the often-quoted 'last years of the 20th century' line does not exist in the film.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: the last fuel → war for it; the oil majors fail

events.title: The last patrol
events.description: The first film's own date, from the Highway 9 sign: Max hunts Toecutter's gang along a coast where the rule of law now depends on a handful of cars.
events.note: On-screen background signage gives 6 December 1984, the franchise's hardest in-universe date.
events.binWhy: The rule of law now depends on a handful of cars.

facets.change: the rule of law → depends on a handful of cars

events.title: The Road Warrior and the last refinery
events.description: Three years on, the wars have gone nuclear: Max trades a tanker of fuel for a tribe of survivors so they can reach the coast, and the world of the first film is gone.
events.note: The three-year gap comes from the official production preamble, not the film; whether the nuclear exchange happens here or between the first two films depends on which continuity you follow.
events.binWhy: The wars have gone nuclear and the world of three years earlier is gone.

facets.change: fuel wars → gone nuclear; the old world gone

events.title: Bartertown and the children of the Crack in the Earth
events.description: Fifteen years after the fuel wars, Sydney is a ruin, a methane town settles its disputes in the Thunderdome, and a tribe of children waits for the pilot who left them in 1999.
events.note: The fifteen-year gap comes from co-writer Terry Hayes (Starlog, June 1985); the film states no year.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: ruins → a methane town with its own law

events.title: Fury Road: the wasteland a generation on
events.description: The franchise's furthest era: a citadel trades water for fuel and chrome, a war rig runs for the green place, and Max's forced tattoo records the day count of a life spent in the wreckage.
events.note: Miller: the apocalypse 'happens, and you wind up 45-50 years in the future' from a rolling 'next Wednesday'; the tattoo implies about thirty-three years since the Fall; the 2015 comics put their Fall in the 2010s. The year is arithmetic on Miller's figure, not a stated date. Furiosa (2024) runs the fifteen years directly into this film.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: wasteland → a citadel trading water for fuel

lineages.groupingNote: Mad Max is the archetype stripped to fuel: the world does not end in a war anyone wins, it runs out of oil, and everything after the first film is set among the wreckage of ordinary Australian life, a police interceptor, a refinery, a ruined Sydney. The fork is dated 1983 with low confidence because the collapse is described only in production and tie-in material, while the films' own dating runs from a title card reading 'a few years from now' to on-screen signage reading 6 December 1984. Tiers: this branch has no T1 and never will, because the franchise's furthest era is the Fury Road wasteland roughly forty-five to fifty years past its Fall, so Mad Max simply stops inside our own next century; the T4 entry is real-world background only (the oil age, 1859), and everything the fiction itself depicts from 1973 onward sits in T3 or T2. Miller's repeated insistence that the films have no strict chronology is the honest summary of this lineage's dates.

lineages.title: Planet of the Apes
lineages.creator: Franklin J. Schaffner (dir.); Michael Wilson & Rod Serling (screenplay), from Pierre Boulle's novel

divergence.label: The plague that kills every dog and cat
divergence.delta: Real: 1983 passes with the world's pets alive and the West rearming; nothing has ended. Fiction: a global plague kills every dog and cat on Earth within months, humans adopt apes as pets and then as slaves, and within a generation the apes have taken the planet.
divergence.note: The pentalogy's first impossible event is actually 1973, when Zira and Cornelius arrive from the destroyed future and Caesar is born, but that is a closed bootstrap loop rather than a break in human history. 1983 is Conquest's 'eight years' before its 1991 uprising and is the first dated alteration to human civilisation; the revolt (1991) and the undated nuclear war are downstream. Confidence is medium because the film supplies only the relative 'eight years ago', not a year.

events.title: On the Origin of Species
events.description: Real history, not fiction: Darwin publishes natural selection, the idea this series literalises by putting apes on top of the pile.
events.note: Real-world background; the fiction itself is silent before 1972.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: fixed species → natural selection published

events.title: The Icarus leaves Earth
events.description: Taylor's ANSA mission launches into the film's own near future, and relativistic time dilation will carry the crew 2,006 years forward while only eighteen months pass for them.
events.note: No on-screen date card. 1972 is derived from the 3978 arrival minus the 2,006 elapsed years the crew log, and from Landon's line about 'the class of '72'.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for territory nobody has reached.

facets.change: Earth → a mission flung two thousand years forward

events.title: Zira and Cornelius land in their own past
events.description: The chimpanzees who fled the destroyed Earth arrive in a recognisable 1973 Los Angeles, testify before a congressional committee and are killed, but their son Caesar survives to close the series' bootstrap loop.
events.note: The first impossible event in the series, but a closed causal loop rather than a change to human history, which is why this lineage's fork is placed at the 1983 plague instead.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: the present → visited by talking apes from a destroyed future

events.title: The plague that kills every dog and cat
events.description: A global plague wipes out the world's dogs and cats within months, humans take apes into their homes as replacements, and the species that will inherit the planet becomes first a pet and then property.
events.note: Conquest gives only the relative 'eight years ago' before its 1991 uprising, so 1983 is arithmetic; the same film is frequently misreported as being set in 1983.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: pets → all dead; apes brought into homes

events.title: Caesar's ape uprising
events.description: The enslaved apes of North America revolt and take the cities, and the human industrial order begins to come apart inside a single generation.
events.note: Conquest's title card gives 1991 and the internal arithmetic fits (Caesar is eighteen, born in 1973), though some timelines read the film as 1993.
events.binWhy: The ruled revolt against those who hold power over them.

facets.change: enslaved apes → take the cities

events.title: The war that ravages the surface
events.description: The human counter-attack becomes the 'vilest war in human history' and leaves the surface a radioactive ruin, which is the world of the Forbidden Zone that Taylor will find.
events.note: Never dated on screen: Battle's Lawgiver places it in the aftermath of Caesar's victory, and that film's 'twelve-year truce' points to about 1992.
events.binWhy: The counter-attack leaves the surface a radioactive ruin.

facets.change: revolt → the counter-attack leaves the surface a ruin

events.title: Ape City and the truce
events.description: A generation after the revolt, Caesar rules a walled ape city where humans and apes are supposed to be equal, and a narrator six centuries later looks back on how fragile that peace was.
events.note: Battle states no year; 'ten years after a worldwide series of ape revolutions and a brutal nuclear war' plus the twelve-year truce puts the main story around 2003, while some sources prefer 2001.
events.binWhy: A truce between species, and a city built on it.

facets.change: war → a walled city and a fragile truce

events.title: The Lawgiver's history lesson
events.description: In 2670 an ape Lawgiver teaches schoolchildren that humans and apes once lived together, which is the ape world's founding myth and the proof that the human past has become scripture.
events.note: On-screen title card 'North America - 2670 A.D.'; the closing line's '600 years after Caesar's death' contradicts the main story's roughly 2003 setting and is unexplained.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: history → taught as scripture

events.title: Two astronauts crash into ape-ruled America
events.description: The 1974 television series drops a pair of twentieth-century astronauts, launched in 1980, into an ape-ruled North America four centuries after the Lawgiver, where humans are mute livestock and fugitives.
events.note: The date is a chronometer reading that the series itself says may have stopped mid-flight; the 1975 animated series is undated, with fans split between 3479 and 3979.
events.binWhy: Twentieth-century astronauts arrive in a future that is not theirs.

facets.change: the present → astronauts land in an ape-ruled future

events.title: Brent arrives and the doomsday bomb ends the Earth
events.description: A second astronaut follows Taylor's trajectory and, days later, the mutant humans of the Forbidden Zone detonate the Alpha-Omega bomb and destroy the planet.
events.note: Brent states 3955 in dialogue while Taylor's chronometer in the 1968 film reads 3978; the standard rationalisation is that Brent's chronometer was damaged.
events.binWhy: An attack or disaster kills on a scale that remakes society.

facets.change: a ruined world → destroyed outright

events.title: Taylor lands on the ape-ruled Earth
events.description: The 1968 film's frame closes as Taylor's ship comes down in the Forbidden Zone, he is hunted and rendered mute, and the half-buried Statue of Liberty reveals that this planet was always Earth.
events.note: The ship's on-screen chronometer reads 3978; the 'November 25' date comes from a later novelisation, not from the film.
events.binWhy: The half-buried statue tells him where he has been all along.

facets.change: a strange planet → recognised as home

lineages.groupingNote: The pentalogy is this archetype's purest long form: a catastrophe inside the twentieth century ends the human industrial order, and the films then live inside its ruins, from a Statue of Liberty on a beach to a sacred scroll that remembers humans as vermin. The fork is placed at the 1983 plague rather than the 1991 uprising because 1983 is the first dated change to human history; the revolt, the war and ape rule are all downstream of it, while the series' earlier impossible event, Zira and Cornelius arriving in 1973, is a closed bootstrap loop rather than a break in human history. Tiers: T4 and T2 are nearly empty because the fiction jumps from the 1990s straight to 2670; the only T4 entry is real-world background (Darwin, 1859) and the only T2 entry is Battle's roughly 2003 setting. T1 is where this branch actually lives, at 2670, 3085, 3955 and 3978. The 2011-2017 reboot (Rise, Dawn, War) and Kingdom (2024) are a separate continuity that re-runs the collapse as a 2016 laboratory accident and a simian-flu pandemic, and the 2001 Burton film is a third; neither is mixed into the events above.

lineages.title: Twelve Monkeys
lineages.creator: Terry Gilliam (dir.); David & Janet Peoples (screenplay), from Chris Marker's La Jetée

divergence.label: The virus is released in Philadelphia
divergence.delta: Real: the winter of 1996 passes with no plague and five billion people live out their lives. Fiction: on 13 December 1996 a laboratory-grown virus is released in Philadelphia, and by 2035 the survivors are sealed underground, sending prisoners back to change a past that cannot be changed.
divergence.note: The 2035 scientists state the date on screen, describing the release as 'probably on December 13, 1996', with symptoms first detected in Philadelphia on 27 December; the film's opening card says five billion will die in 1997.

events.title: The Russian flu pandemic
events.description: Real history, not fiction: a respiratory pandemic rides the new railway and steamship networks out of Central Asia and kills about a million people, the real rehearsal for the fiction's plague.
events.note: Real-world background; death tolls vary by source.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: new railways → a pandemic rides them

events.title: The first jump lands in the First World War
events.description: A targeting error drops Cole into a trench in 1917, where he is shot in the leg, a wound that will still be in his thigh when he reaches 1996.
events.note: On screen; the bullet is the object half of the film's time loop.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: a trench → a man from the future lands in it

events.title: La Jetée
events.description: Chris Marker's photo-roman tells the same story with no dates at all, a man from a post-war underground sent back to a woman on a pier, and gives Gilliam's film its structure and its ending.
events.note: Real-world publication; La Jetée never dates its Third World War or its future.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The second jump lands in 1990
events.description: Sent to 1996, Cole arrives six years early, is arrested, and meets Jeffrey Goines and Dr Railly in a Baltimore asylum, seeding the false lead that runs through the rest of the film.
events.note: Railly states 'This is 1990'; the opening title card is dated 12 April 1990.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: an asylum → a man from the future, six years early

events.title: The virus is released, and the loop closes
events.description: Cole's jump lands in November 1996 and in December he is shot dead at Philadelphia airport in front of his own child self while Dr Peters walks onto a plane carrying the virus, so the plague is not prevented but caused.
events.note: The 2035 scientists state the release date on screen; the Army of the Twelve Monkeys, whose name they blame, are animal-rights activists and a red herring, and the carrier is Goines's assistant, Dr Peters.
