whereToStart.blurb: Chris Marker's twenty-eight-minute photo-roman, the source of the story and its ending.

whereToStart.title: Twelve Monkeys
whereToStart.blurb: A separate continuity with different rules; not part of this lineage.

connections.note: Both send a man back to stop a catastrophe his own mission may be helping to cause.
Both futures treat people as raw material: convicts as scouts, bodies as batteries.
Both begin in a recognisable twentieth century and end in the ruins of it.

worlds.setting: On Saturday 23 October 2077 the bombs fell and the world ended in about two hours. The America that died had never moved past the 1950s: it was a country of diners, atomic cars, civil-defence drills and cheerful corporate advertising, and its ruins are still full of all three - robots polishing floors, broadcasters reading old news, billboards for products nobody makes. The survivors came out of Vault-Tec vaults that were never really shelters: each vault was a secret sociological experiment performed on the people sealed inside.
worlds.conflict: The old world will not stay dead and the new one cannot agree on what to build. The Enclave claims to be the legitimate United States, the Brotherhood of Steel wants dangerous technology locked away, the Institute manufactures synthetic people, and the New California Republic is attempting a republic. Everyone with a plan turns out to be running an experiment on somebody, which is the wasteland's one reliable political tradition.
worlds.politics: No government survives the war. What replaces it is a patchwork: the New California Republic with a senate and a bureaucracy, Caesar's Legion as a slaver army modelled on Rome, the Brotherhood of Steel as a militarised technology cult, and the Enclave as the pre-war state's surviving remnant. Vault-Tec's contracts and old corporate AIs still exercise power long after the country that chartered them ceased to exist.
worlds.technology: Retro-futurist and broken: fusion-powered cars, laser and plasma weapons, Power Armor, robots with personalities, and computers that run on tape and green text. Everything is 1950s Americana with atomic power, and everything is falling apart, so the economy runs on bottle caps and the most valuable skill is knowing how to repair the twentieth century.
worlds.mood: Satirical, brutal, absurd - the end of the world with a jukebox playing, where horror and comedy arrive in the same scene.

locations.name: The Vaults
locations.blurb: Sealed shelters built by Vault-Tec as experiments, opened decades later on schedule or by accident.

locations.name: The Capital Wasteland

locations.name: New Vegas and Hoover Dam

locations.name: The Commonwealth

factions.name: The Brotherhood of Steel
factions.blurb: A knightly order descended from an army mutineer, hoarding technology to keep it from everyone.

factions.name: The Enclave
factions.blurb: The pre-war government's remnant, insisting it is still the United States and acting accordingly.

factions.name: The New California Republic
factions.blurb: A real republic with a senate, a flag and more bureaucracy than it can afford.

factions.name: Caesar's Legion
factions.blurb: A slaver army modelled on Rome, which considers democracy a weakness and says so.

whereToStart.title: Fallout
whereToStart.blurb: The Amazon series: the most accessible way in, and canon to the games.

whereToStart.title: Fallout 4
whereToStart.blurb: A pre-war father wakes in the ruins of Boston; the friendliest modern entry point.

whereToStart.title: Fallout
whereToStart.blurb: The original: isometric, bleak, and the source of the Vaults and the Master.

connections.note: The two poles of post-apocalyptic fiction: austere Australia against Fallout's satirical, over-stuffed wasteland.
Both end the world with a nuclear exchange; one blames the machines, one blames the powers.
Both build a future on the radioactive ruins of the twentieth century and its buried monuments.

worlds.setting: Most human beings live in a city that looks like 1999 and cannot leave it: offices, payphones, noodle bars, the same year running on a loop, with work, rent and weather. Their bodies lie in pods and their heat is fed into the machines' power supply, and almost nobody inside knows. The simulation is not a puzzle or a prison; it is a place to live, built to be believed. Outside, the sky is black with nanites and the last free city is underground.
worlds.conflict: The machines need the pods to keep running and the people inside them docile, so the system is built to be believed; the humans who wake up need it destroyed, so the war is fought over what people will accept as real. Every cycle the machines offer one chosen person the same bargain, and every cycle the resistance must decide whether freeing humanity is worth ending it.
worlds.politics: The Machines are the state: a city of programs that governs a farm of human beings, with the Architect, the Oracle and the central intelligence managing the simulation and its cycles. Among humans, Zion is a militarised city-state run by a council and its ship captains, and the rogue programs inside the Matrix - exiles, Agents, the Merovingian - have a politics of their own that matters more than any human government.
worlds.technology: Inside, the technology is exactly 1999: landlines, pagers, CRT monitors and hard-wired telephones, because the simulation was built from the last human world and never updated. Outside, the real world runs on hovercraft, EMP weapons and pods; the machines build in black chrome, and the most powerful tool anyone has is the ability to rewrite the simulation's rules from within it.
worlds.mood: Cool, paranoid, vertiginous - a martial-arts action film with a philosophy seminar underneath and a permanently black sky overhead.
themes: the chosen one as a mechanism

locations.name: The Matrix
locations.blurb: The simulated city of 1999, where nearly everyone lives and nothing is what it appears.

locations.name: The pod fields
locations.blurb: The towers where human beings are grown, kept alive and harvested for power.

locations.name: Zion
locations.blurb: The last free human city, built deep underground and permanently preparing for attack.

locations.name: Zero One

factions.name: The Machines
factions.blurb: The ruling intelligence and its programs, which farm human beings and prefer consent to force.

factions.name: The Agents
factions.blurb: System programs that police the simulation, able to overwrite anyone still plugged in.

factions.name: The Resistance
factions.blurb: Zion's captains and their crews, running hovercraft into the Matrix to wake people up.

factions.name: The exiles
factions.blurb: Programs that refused deletion, from the Oracle to the Merovingian's smuggling operation.

whereToStart.title: The Matrix
whereToStart.blurb: The original: everything you need to understand the world is in it.

whereToStart.title: The Animatrix
whereToStart.blurb: Nine animated shorts, including the Second Renaissance history of the machine war.

whereToStart.title: The Matrix Resurrections
whereToStart.blurb: Sixty years on, and only worth it after the first three films.

connections.note: Machine rule two ways: Skynet's open extermination against the Matrix's quiet farm.
Both end with a revelation about what humanity actually is and who is really in charge.
Dick's nested realities are the Matrix's ancestors: a true world hidden behind a false one.

worlds.setting: Late-1990s America, exactly as it was: the Very Large Array in New Mexico, NASA budget fights, SETI kept alive on private grants, cable news and religious broadcasting. The single change is a signal - a repeating prime number from Vega, twenty-six light years out, carrying a 1936 Olympic broadcast and then sixty-three thousand pages of engineering drawings. Governments build the machine those drawings specify, and the novel and the film resolve the ride differently. The story covers about three years.
worlds.conflict: The engine is an argument, not an invasion: what counts as evidence, and who is allowed to hold it. Scientists, soldiers and preachers read the same signal and reach different conclusions, and the machine turns a private obsession into a public referendum - on whether humanity is alone, whether faith and reason can share a room, and who gets to speak for the species.
worlds.politics: The signal runs through ordinary 1990s institutions: a White House that wants a usable answer, a security apparatus that wants the machine under its control, and an international consortium that finishes a second one in Hokkaido. Around them, millenarian cults and mainstream clergy fight the meaning out in public.
worlds.technology: Present-day and unfashionably so: radio telescopes, tape archives, room-sized supercomputers, Space Shuttle hardware, and one alien machine - concentric rings and a single seat, with no engine anyone can identify. There is no starship, no fleet and no invasion; the wonder is a wormhole with a fixed itinerary, and a chair that falls through it.
worlds.mood: Sober, hopeful, argumentative. It is the most procedural of first-contact stories - the awe is filtered through funding hearings, security briefings and live television - and its most affecting scenes are about a daughter and her dead father, not a spacecraft.
themes: faith and reason in one room
grief and the search for a parent

locations.name: The Very Large Array, New Mexico
locations.blurb: A field of steerable dishes where the prime numbers arrive and a career is made and unmade.

locations.name: Cape Canaveral
locations.blurb: The film's site for the first machine; the novel builds the same machine in Wyoming instead.

locations.name: Hokkaido
locations.blurb: The second machine, funded internationally and built in secret, and the one that carries a passenger.

locations.name: The station at the galactic centre
locations.blurb: Where the machine delivers its passenger: built for visitors by whoever sent the message.

factions.name: Ellie Arroway's SETI team
factions.blurb: A handful of researchers living on private grants, one budget vote away from being shut down.

factions.name: The American government
factions.blurb: Takes the signal over, wants the machine under military control, and owns the official record.

factions.name: The Hokkaido consortium
factions.blurb: The international funders who build the surviving machine after the first one is destroyed.

factions.name: The religious opposition
factions.blurb: Millenarian movements and mainstream clergy who read the signal as revelation, blasphemy or a test.

factions.name: The senders
factions.blurb: Whoever transmitted from Vega, twenty-six light years away and never met as themselves.

whereToStart.title: Contact
whereToStart.blurb: Zemeckis's film, the version most people meet first and the one this lineage's dates follow.

whereToStart.title: Contact
whereToStart.blurb: Sagan's novel: the same signal, a Machine built in Wyoming, and a final chapter the film drops.

connections.note: Both send one traveller out and bring them back with an experience nobody else can verify.
Both are one trip to a signal or wormhole, and both are really about a parent and child.
The 1990s' other signal story: Contact puts the evidence on television, The X-Files locks it away.

worlds.setting: Everything familiar is the 1960s' idea of 2001: Pan Am shuttles to a wheel-shaped space station, a Hilton hotel in orbit, videophone calls home, and a permanent American base at Clavius. The single change is an object. A black slab buried four million years ago near Tycho is dug up on the Moon and answers the sunrise with one radio pulse aimed at Jupiter. The story then runs from tool-using australopithecines to a finale the film declines to explain.
worlds.conflict: The engine is not a war but a question of agency: something older and far more capable has been shaping humans since before they were human, and it never explains itself. Every advance - the first tool, HAL's patient voice, Bowman's transit - happens inside a design whose plans nobody on screen is allowed to see. People act, and cannot tell whether they chose.
worlds.politics: An American-led space programme holds the Moon and the Jupiter mission, briefs its own people on a cover story and answers to a civilian authority the audience never meets; the only other power on screen is a courteous Soviet delegation kept outside the secret. There is no war and no ideology - the authority that actually shapes events is non-human, off-stage and four million years old.
worlds.technology: The near-future as 1968 imagined it: reusable shuttles, a rotating station that supplies gravity, hibernation pods, voice-print doors, and HAL, a computer that talks, reads lips and runs the ship. What is absent is the real twenty-first century - no internet culture, no personal computing, no digital clutter. The monoliths are the only magic, and they are never explained.
worlds.mood: Cold, serene, ceremonial. Terror and wonder arrive at the same temperature: the film's most violent act is committed by a polite voice, and its ending offers transcendence without consolation.
themes: tools and the species that makes them
intelligence that will not explain itself

locations.name: TMA-1, near Tycho
locations.blurb: A slab buried four million years ago, dug up under a press blackout, and the reason for everything after.

locations.name: Clavius Base

locations.name: Space Station V

locations.name: Discovery One

locations.name: The Star Gate

factions.name: The makers of the monoliths

whereToStart.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
whereToStart.blurb: The film itself, and the only version that matters: see it before reading anything about it.

whereToStart.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
whereToStart.blurb: Clarke's parallel novel, written alongside the film, answers questions the film deliberately leaves open.

whereToStart.title: 2010: The Year We Make Contact
whereToStart.blurb: The sequel that explains the first film's ending and turns silence into a much chattier kind of story.

connections.note: The other great hard-science cosmic film, and its mirror: Kubrick withholds the meaning, Nolan explains his.
Both send one traveller out and bring them back with an experience nobody else can verify.
The same optimistic 1960s space future, stripped of camaraderie, explanation and any human in charge.

worlds.setting: Britain in 2027, and it is recognisably ours with the volume turned down: buses, coffee shops, council flats, and a state of emergency so old it has become weather. The single change is biological - humanity became infertile in 2009, and no child has been born in eighteen years. Britain has sealed itself and turned on the refugees it has interned. The film covers a few weeks of that eighteenth year; P. D. James's novel set the same collapse in 1995 and its story in 2021.
worlds.conflict: The engine is not a war but a slow failure of maintenance: a species with no future going through the motions of a state, and the question of what hope does to people who have none. The immediate fight is over one pregnant woman - who gets to own her, protect her or use her - but the deeper conflict is between those who accept extinction and those who cannot.
worlds.politics: A British state under emergency rule has suspended the ordinary rules: Homeland Security runs identity checks, detention and deportation, refugees are held behind wire at Bexhill, and the only armed opposition is a small underground of former activists. There is nowhere to appeal and nowhere to go - the rest of the world is in worse shape, and Britain says so constantly.
worlds.technology: Exactly the technology of 2006, with a few additions the crisis produced: walled compounds, CCTV, armoured buses, and Quietus, a suicide kit sold openly in shops. Everything works slightly worse than it used to - the trains run, the phones work, the buildings are grimy - and nothing futuristic has arrived to help. The one piece of magic is the Human Project, a scientific refuge in the Azores that may not exist.
worlds.mood: Exhausted, grey, tender. The dominant note is not panic but the fatigue of people who have been grieving for eighteen years; the film is full of coughs, plastic sheeting and grim courtesy, and its most shocking moments are small acts of tenderness in places built to prevent them.

locations.name: London
locations.blurb: A functioning city of checkpoints, screens and anti-terror advertising, where emergency has become routine.

locations.name: Bexhill-on-Sea
locations.blurb: The internment camp on the south coast where Britain keeps its refugees caged behind wire, indefinitely.

locations.name: The Ark of the Arts
locations.blurb: Battersea Power Station, filled with the world's art treasures and kept for an audience that will never come.

locations.name: Jasper's farmhouse

locations.name: The Azores
locations.blurb: The rumoured home of the Human Project, the last scientific refuge anyone in Britain still talks about.

factions.name: The British state
factions.blurb: Emergency government, Homeland Security, checkpoints and deportation: order maintained by treating refugees as the enemy.

factions.name: The Fishes
factions.blurb: A small armed underground of former activists, split between idealism and people who want power.

factions.name: The Human Project
factions.blurb: A rumoured scientific refuge abroad that the world's last hope is quietly pinned on.

factions.name: The last generation
factions.blurb: Everyone born in or before 2009: a whole society with no children in it, ageing together.

whereToStart.title: Children of Men
whereToStart.blurb: Cuaron's film, which this world is drawn from: short, relentless, and almost never explains itself.

whereToStart.title: The Children of Men
whereToStart.blurb: P. D. James's novel: the same infertility, an England twenty-six years in, and a very different ending.

connections.note: Both imagine humanity's continuation managed by a system: the Matrix farms people, Britain interns them.
Both are stories of a species with no future on its own planet: one lost to infertility, one to blight.
Both are end-of-the-species stories set off by a biological accident that nobody can undo.

worlds.setting: Dust-bowl farm country in the American interior, and it looks like the 1930s with better machines: combines, ballgames on a screen, a school that teaches the Moon landings were faked to bankrupt the Soviets. The single change is a blight. Wheat went first, then okra, and corn is going; the species is being starved off its own planet. The only way out is a wormhole near Saturn, found in 2019. The film's timeline then stretches a century, most of it lost to relativity.
worlds.conflict: The engine is not an enemy but a deadline: a species that has run out of time on its own planet, arguing about how to spend what is left. The choice is between rescuing everyone alive now and planting a colony for a generation nobody will live to meet. Every relationship in the film is a parent and child separated by that arithmetic.
worlds.politics: Thin by design. Government has shrunk to local schools, a shuttered space programme and a sheriff, and what remains of NASA is hidden in a bunker, because for a generation the schools have taught that leaving the planet was waste. Order is kept by habit, dust masks and rationing, and the only institution with real authority is the one nobody is allowed to know still exists.
worlds.technology: Salvaged twentieth-century: pickup trucks, combines, crop-survey drones whose solar cells are worth stealing, radios carried into the fields. Spaceflight hardware is old and precious, flown by pilots trained before the collapse; the internet texture of our century is gone and messages arrive as stored video that piles up unwatched. Time itself becomes the most expensive thing the technology spends.
worlds.mood: Elegiac, dusty, stubborn. The dominant feeling is not fear but grief for a world already lost; the film keeps its most emotional scenes in kitchens and truck cabs, and its awe is a small ship alone against a very large silence.
themes: leaving rather than saving the world

locations.name: The Cooper farm

locations.name: Gargantua

factions.name: The Endurance crew

factions.name: The farm towns

whereToStart.title: Interstellar
whereToStart.blurb: The film itself: nearly three hours, and the only version of this story that exists.

whereToStart.title: The Science of Interstellar
whereToStart.blurb: Kip Thorne's companion volume explains the physics on screen, and supplies the dates the film never states.

connections.note: The other great hard-science cosmic film, and its mirror: Kubrick withholds meaning, Nolan explains his.
Both are one trip to a signal or wormhole, and both come down to a parent and child separated.
Both are end-of-the-biosphere stories about a species with no future, one from blight, one from infertility.

worlds.setting: Two centuries after a fusion drive opened the solar system, the familiar is still in place: an overcrowded Earth of thirty billion governed by the UN, a Mars settled in 2050 and generations into making a dead planet live, and a Belt of stations whose people mine the ice and metal that keep both alive and are treated as colonial labour. The single change is the Epstein Drive. There is no artificial gravity: ships burn halfway, flip, and burn again. The story opens in 2350 and spans centuries.
worlds.conflict: The engine is a colonial economy with three claimants and no exit: Earth needs the Belt's resources and holds the purse, Mars needs Earth's and resents the dependency, and the Belt does the dying work while being taxed, policed and called ungrateful. Every crisis runs through that structure - water riots, blockades, a stolen warship - and the alien substance on Phoebe only accelerates a fight that was already coming.
worlds.politics: Power sits with two governments and a diaspora: the UN on Earth, whose elections the off-worlders cannot vote in, and the Martian Congressional Republic, a militarised meritocracy where citizenship is earned through service and the terraforming project is the point of the nation. The Belt has no sovereign state of its own, only the Outer Planets Alliance - a union, a lobby and, at times, an armed movement that Earth and Mars both call terrorism.
worlds.technology: Hard, dirty, plausible engineering: fusion drives under months-long burn, patched vacuum suits, mag-boots instead of gravity, hand terminals that float data in the air, rail guns, torpedoes and point-defence cannons. Nothing is sleek. Air and water are metered, gravity is something only a spinning station or a burning drive provides, and the only truly incomprehensible thing in the system is the alien substance recovered from Phoebe - an artefact that treats living tissue as raw material and has no mind to negotiate with.
worlds.mood: Grubby, proud, claustrophobic. It plays as a western and a labour dispute in vacuum: people drinking in station bars under a dome, one hull breach from dying, and entirely certain that the inner planets will never see them as anything but hired help.
themes: us and them across a vacuum
found family on a borrowed ship

locations.name: Ceres Station
locations.blurb: The Belt's port city inside a spun-up asteroid, where air and water are sold by the litre.

locations.name: Tycho Station
locations.blurb: The largest mobile construction platform in the system, and the yard building the Nauvoo.

locations.name: Earth
locations.blurb: Thirty billion people under UN rule, most of them on Basic assistance, in a climate-stressed world.

locations.name: Mars
locations.blurb: A planet mid-terraform: dome cities, a serious navy, and people who expect to see open air.

locations.name: Ganymede

factions.blurb: Governs thirty billion people, controls the shipping lanes, and treats the Belt as a restive colony.

factions.name: Martian Congressional Republic
factions.blurb: A meritocracy built on terraforming, with the system's best navy and citizenship earned by service.

factions.name: Outer Planets Alliance
factions.blurb: The Belt's fractious movement - union, lobby and armed faction at once - which Earth calls terrorism.

factions.name: Star Helix Security
factions.blurb: The private police force contracted to keep order on Ceres, and resented by everyone there.

factions.name: The Mormon expedition
factions.blurb: A religious group building a generation ship at Tycho to leave the solar system entirely.

whereToStart.title: Leviathan Wakes
whereToStart.blurb: The first novel and the clearest way in: a missing woman, an ice hauler, and politics from the bottom.

whereToStart.title: The Expanse
whereToStart.blurb: Six seasons on screen and the easiest way to feel the physics; season one covers the first book.

connections.note: Routinely described as the answer to Star Trek's post-scarcity idealism: same ambition, none of the comfort.
An acknowledged influence on the authors: Asimov's political scale, redrawn inside a single solar system.
Both are resource politics in space, and both turn on a substance that rewrites what a human being is.

worlds.setting: The galaxy is a web of hyperlanes linking thousands of inhabited worlds, all of it governed badly from the city-planet Coruscant. Ordinary life stays local: a moisture farmer on Tatooine sells water to survive, a freighter crew runs cargo past Imperial patrols, a mechanic keeps droids running on a backwater moon. Above them the Republic rots into an Empire, the Empire collapses into warlord remnants, and the cycle begins again under the First Order.
worlds.conflict: The engine is a fight over who governs the galaxy and by what right. A Republic of worlds becomes an Empire under one Sith Lord; a rebellion restores a New Republic that disarms too soon; the Imperial remnant returns as the First Order. The Jedi, once the Republic's peacekeepers, are hunted to near-extinction and remembered as a rumour.
worlds.politics: Power is whoever holds Coruscant: the Senate and a Supreme Chancellor in the Republic's last centuries, then the Emperor with his Moffs and planetary governors, then a quarrelling New Republic. What actually reaches any single planet is decided lower down, by sector governors, Hutt crime families and shipping cartels.
worlds.technology: Hyperdrives cross the galaxy in hours; droids do the labour; blasters, repulsorlift speeders and cybernetic prosthetics are ordinary, and a farm kid can rebuild a droid from scrap. What is missing is the network: no internet, no planetary data web, no way to look anything up. News arrives by HoloNet broadcast, courier or not at all, and outer worlds live on rumour.
worlds.mood: Worn-in, romantic, elegiac. The galaxy is dusty and second-hand - cantinas, salvage yards, freighters held together with tape - while the moral stakes stay enormous, and a choice made in a nowhere town decides the fate of worlds.

locations.name: Coruscant
locations.blurb: Planet-wide capital: Jedi Temple, Senate chamber, and later the Imperial Palace all sit here.

locations.name: Tatooine
locations.blurb: Desert world of moisture farms, salvage and gangsters; where the story starts and keeps returning.

locations.name: Alderaan
locations.blurb: Core world of diplomats and pacifists, destroyed outright as a demonstration of Imperial power.

locations.name: Hoth
locations.blurb: Frozen, nearly empty world; the Rebel Alliance's hidden base and the Empire's counterstroke.

locations.name: The Outer Rim
locations.blurb: Frontier of small settlements and no law, where the Republic's writ barely runs.

factions.name: The Jedi Order
factions.blurb: Monastic peacekeepers who use the Force; generals in the Clone Wars, then hunted almost to extinction.

factions.name: The Galactic Empire
factions.blurb: Palpatine's military state of Moffs, stormtroopers and Star Destroyers; disarmed at Jakku, reborn as the First Order.

factions.name: The Rebel Alliance
factions.blurb: Coalition of rebel cells and defectors fighting to restore the Republic.

factions.name: The Sith
factions.blurb: Ancient order of Force-users devoted to domination, working through a master and one apprentice.

factions.name: The Hutts
factions.blurb: Crime families controlling a stretch of the Outer Rim through debt, slavery and smuggling.

whereToStart.title: Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope
whereToStart.blurb: The original entry point: Empire, Rebellion and the Force in one self-contained story.

whereToStart.title: Star Wars Rebels
whereToStart.blurb: Shows ordinary life under Imperial occupation on one backwater planet.

whereToStart.title: Lost Stars
whereToStart.blurb: Two friends on opposite sides of the civil war; the clearest view of Imperial service.

connections.note: Space opera's two poles: Star Wars is a mythic past, Star Trek an institutional future.
Both give a feudal galaxy, a spice trade and a desert messiah; Dune is the political version.
Both stage a galactic empire's fall and return; Foundation computes it, Star Wars mythologises it.

worlds.setting: Earth has no money, no hunger and no want, and its people join a fleet out of interest rather than wages. This is the leading world of the United Federation of Planets, a union of some hundred and fifty member worlds from Vulcan to Andoria and Tellar, with Starfleet as its exploring and fighting arm. Most citizens never leave their homeworld; those who do serve on starships, on starbases like Deep Space Nine, or in frontier colonies.
worlds.conflict: The Federation believes force is a last resort and keeps testing that belief against powers that do not: Klingons, Romulans, Cardassians and the Dominion, which nearly wins. Its internal argument is the Prime Directive, which forbids interference in other cultures and gets broken whenever a crew decides the rule is wrong.
worlds.politics: A civilian Federation Council and President, drawn from member worlds, set policy, and Starfleet answers to them in theory; its own admiralty has started wars and covered them up. Beyond the border sit the Klingon Empire, the Romulan Star Empire and the Cardassian Union, and by the 25th century the Romulan state is a ruin.
worlds.technology: Warp drive, transporters, replicators, universal translators and holodecks; medicine cures most disease and repairs most injuries. Federation ships carry no cloaking device, by treaty; human genetic engineering is illegal after the Eugenics Wars; and the Prime Directive limits what technology may be handed to anyone else. All of it depends on dilithium, and in the 31st century the galaxy's supply is destroyed in an instant.
worlds.mood: Optimistic, procedural, argumentative. Clean, well-lit ships crewed by professionals who solve problems by talking, and the drama comes from whether their ethics survive a situation that does not reward them.

worlds.setting: A million human worlds pay tithes to the Imperium of Man, whose ruler has sat dead but not dead on the Golden Throne on Terra for ten thousand years. Ordinary life is a hive city: shifts in a manufactorum, corpse-starch rations, a chapel on every level, and a governor whose one duty is the Imperial tithe. Above that the Administratum, the Ecclesiarchy and the Astra Militarum grind on enormously, slowly and half-mad. The Great Rift has torn the galaxy in two.
worlds.conflict: The Imperium is permanently at war with everything: Orks, Aeldari, Tyranids, Necrons, Chaos and its own rebels, on a scale where a lost regiment is a rounding error. The deeper conflict is that the system keeping humanity alive is the same system that keeps it ignorant and cruel, and every alternative on offer is extinction or corruption. Nothing improves.
worlds.politics: The Emperor is a comatose figurehead who is also officially a god, and real power sits with the High Lords of Terra and the great institutions: the Ecclesiarchy, the Inquisition, the Adeptus Mechanicus, the Astra Militarum, the Navis Nobilite. Since the Great Rift the returned primarch Roboute Guilliman has ruled as Lord Commander, and no faction can reform any of it.
worlds.technology: Nothing has been invented for ten thousand years. Technology is a religion: the Mechanicus of Mars copies Standard Template Construct designs it no longer understands, blesses its machines before use and calls innovation heresy. Ships cross the warp, a hostile dimension where time runs wrong and daemons wait, guided by a mutant navigator caste, and messages travel as dreams sent by astropaths. Artificial intelligence is banned absolutely.
worlds.mood: Gothic, vast, oppressive, and blackly funny. Cathedrals the size of cities, skulls on every surface, incense and propaganda laid over machinery that kills the people operating it, and an administration so large it has lost worlds from its own records.

worlds.setting: Ten thousand years after the Butlerian Jihad, humanity lives in a feudal Imperium of Great Houses under one Emperor, and the whole thing runs on a single commodity: the spice melange, harvested on the desert planet Arrakis, which extends life, opens prescience and lets the Spacing Guild's navigators fold space. Ordinary people live under a House, a Guild contract or a CHOAM charter. On Arrakis they wear stillsuits that recycle every drop of body water, and water is money.
worlds.conflict: The engine is scarcity and control: whoever controls spice controls interstellar travel, and therefore the Imperium. Around that sit the Great Convention's rules for war, the Bene Gesserit breeding programme, and the Fremen, a desert people the Imperium has spent generations dismissing. The Atreides arrive on Arrakis, are destroyed there, and produce a messiah whose jihad kills billions.
worlds.politics: The Emperor rules through the Landsraad of Great Houses, but real power is a balance of three: the Emperor's Sardaukar legions, the Spacing Guild's monopoly on transport, and CHOAM, the cartel holding every commercial licence. The Bene Gesserit sisterhood works above all three, placing its people in every great house.
worlds.technology: No computers and no thinking machines: the Butlerian Jihad made that religious law, so calculation is done by human minds trained as Mentats. Holtzman shields make bullets useless, so wars are fought with knives and decided by training, and atomics exist but the Great Convention forbids using them on people. Interstellar travel belongs to the Guild alone, and nobody else can navigate.
worlds.mood: Dry, fatalistic, immense. Heat, thirst, ritual and long plotting; the books read like an anthropologist's report on a religion being born, with a warning underneath about the leaders it produces.

worlds.setting: Trantor is one city wrapped around a planet: forty billion people who never see open sky, eating food shipped in from twenty agricultural worlds, running the administration of an empire of millions of worlds. Further out the Empire is a memory thinning into superstition - a province like Anacreon is a kingdom with atomic heaters and nobody left who can repair them. On Terminus, at the rim, a small colony of scientists is compiling an encyclopedia.
worlds.conflict: The Empire is falling and cannot be argued out of it; the Foundation's purpose is not to prevent the fall but to shorten the dark age after it from thirty thousand years to one thousand. Each crisis is a problem with one correct answer, solved by politics, religion or trade rather than force - until the Mule, who is not in the equations at all.
worlds.politics: A hereditary Emperor on Trantor rules through a colossal civil service, while the Commission of Public Safety and the military decide more each century and outer provinces drift into hereditary kingdoms. The Foundation is run by mayors and traders, and behind it a Second Foundation of psychologists corrects what the First Foundation cannot see.
worlds.technology: Atomic power is the load-bearing technology: Trantor is heated and fed by atomic plants, and the Foundation's first export is a nuclear power station sold to a kingdom that can no longer build one. Hyperspace crosses the galaxy in days; personal shields, blasters and microfilm are ordinary. There are no aliens anywhere in the galaxy, no robots in the original stories, and psychohistory is mathematics done by people, not machines.
worlds.mood: Cool, procedural, elegiac. Decline is recorded as an administrative fact - reports, trade delegations, a shrinking map - and the pleasure is watching clever people solve a crisis with the tools they have.

news.headline: Artemis II splashes down after a crewed lunar flyby
news.summary: Four astronauts flew around the Moon and back, the first crewed flight beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17 in 1972. It is the first crewed flight of the Space Launch System and of the Orion spacecraft.

news.headline: First landing near the lunar south pole
news.summary: India's Chandrayaan-3 puts a lander and rover down at high southern latitude, where water ice is expected in permanently shadowed craters. The date is now marked as National Space Day in India.

news.headline: A fusion experiment returns more energy than it absorbed
news.summary: The National Ignition Facility achieves scientific breakeven for the first time, with a gain factor of about 1.5. The reaction lasted a fraction of a second and is a long way from a power station.

atlas.title: Where We Are Now - a converging timeline of science fiction
atlas.headline: Every one of these histories
atlas.lede: Twenty-four science-fiction worlds, each pinned to the **real calendar** rather than its own. Every one of them rode along our history, broke away at one dated moment, and is drawn right up to the line where ==we are now==. Grouped by **how** they break with us rather than by genre - because that is what decides whether a world is hiding underneath this one, downstream of a war we won, or waiting ten thousand years ahead.
atlas.futureLabel: the future →   the years none of us have reached
atlas.legendHint: drag to pan · scroll to zoom · click a branch or card to enter that world

distribution.title: Where the charted time actually sits
distribution.blurb: Each world's recorded events, bucketed by when they land on the real calendar. The vertical rule is today: bars starting to its left are stories that begin in our past, and a long right tail means the fiction runs deep into the future.

worlds.title: Enter a world
worlds.blurb: Every card opens the full dossier: what the place is like to live in, who holds power, what the technology does and conspicuously refuses to do, where to begin, and which other worlds it genuinely connects to.

notes.heading: How this was built, and what to distrust
paragraphs: **The conversion problem.** Only some of these fictions date themselves in real years. Star Trek does - first contact is 5 April 2063. Everything else had to be converted: Star Wars counts from the Battle of Yavin, Dune counts After Guild, Foundation counts Galactic Era, Warhammer counts millennia. Read those positions as *projections*, not recorded history. Every event keeps its original in-universe label so you can check the arithmetic yourself.

**Star Wars really does land in the deep past.** Its own opening says "a long time ago", and converting BBY against a 1977 anchor puts the founding of the Republic around 23,000 BCE. That is not a sign error, and every world carries an *epoch* field saying which way it faces.

**The axis is warped.** The dataset runs from roughly 2 billion BCE to 48,000 CE, so the scale is a symmetric log: it stretches the centuries around now and compresses deep time, staying continuous and monotonic throughout. Year labels are exact; spacing is not. *Full reach* is the widest honest window.

**Confidence is recorded per event.** High means the fiction states it outright; medium means it was inferred or computed from a stated anchor; low means sources genuinely conflict - usually a book-versus-film or canon-level disagreement - and the competing claim is written out in the event note rather than quietly resolved.

**Editing it.** The dataset lives beside this file: one JSON file per archetype under `data/parts/`, world dossiers under `data/parts/worlds/`, the page copy in `data/atlas.json`, and the contract in `data/SCHEMA.md`. Run `python3 build-data.py` to validate and rebuild; it refuses to build on bad data, assembles the viewer from `src/`, and embeds the result here.
